subject: beetle
reasoning:
I'm planning the stag beetle's proportions and scale, aiming for a realistic size around 8cm long with the body facing forward, and starting to map out the skeleton structure with thorax, head, and jaw segments.

Now I'm defining joints and placements for the legs, antennae, elytra, and abdomen, using coxa-femur-tibia-tarsus chains for each of the six legs and hinged mandible chains for the mouthparts, all positioned in meter-scale coordinates with the body elevated above the ground.

Writing mandible geometry...

Now I'm setting up the elytra as hinged shell halves: scaled sphere shapes positioned at the front edge with a hinge joint, plus an abdomen sphere underneath to fill out the body shape.

Still shaping body parts...

Working out leg placement next: six legs total, three per side with hip, knee, and foot points positioned along the body at varying z-depths, using simple explicit joint coordinates rather than full IK.

I'll use polylines for the legs so sweep rounds the joints with fillets, varying the radius along the leg to taper toward the tip. I'm adding small spikes along the tibia and a tiny claw spike at the tarsal tip, with the foot resting just above y=0 to simulate a slight ground contact sink.

I need to check overall body height against the elytra and abdomen placement to make sure everything stacks correctly above the floor. For parenting, I'll attach spikes to the chain's bone points using their frame weights, and set mandibles to parent off the head joint while front legs parent to the thorax and mid/back legs to the body—making sure joints are created in root-first order.

Setting up the body skeleton: body, thorax, head, jaw, and abdomen joints with spine roles, plus hinge joints for the elytra. I'm placing a small jaw/labium part under the mouth, a labrum box above it, and tiny palp spheres, then positioning the elytra joints and their spherical shell parts so the overall body length stretches from the mandible tips in front back through the abdomen.

Realizing the total length (~0.11-0.125) is a bit oversized even for a large stag beetle, so I'm defining a uniform scale factor to shrink all coordinates proportionally. I'm setting up a helper function using a scale constant around 0.0008 to convert my millimeter-based measurements down to the right size, applying it to both positions and radii consistently.

Working through the body plan in mm units: abdomen, thorax, head, and jaw joints positioned along the spine, then placing the abdomen sphere, left/right elytra spheres with slight overlap at the midline, and considering countershading paint and a seam ridge along the elytra to suggest the beetle's wing case division.

I'm also sketching the pronotum as a scaled sphere over the thorax, the head with wide temple bulges suited to a stag beetle's build, and positioning the eye spheres near the sides of the head.

Now I'm building out the mandibles as a swept chain of decreasing radii from base to tip with a dark glossy color, adding inward-pointing teeth spikes at specific points along the curve.

For antennae, I'm defining a chain of named joints as a polyline sweeping to thinner radii, then adding club-shaped plate segments at the tip rotated to match the antenna's direction.

Still defining antenna plates...

Joint 0 is at the hip and joint 1 at the knee, confirming the leg chain works for the rest pose. I'm adding a ventral thorax sphere for a lighter underside tone, and considering whether to skip extra pronotum details to keep things simple, while reusing a single shared sphere geometry across parts for efficiency.

Setting up the builder, defining joints with parent/dir/role for body and thorax, writing a sphere helper function, and starting the leg-building loop with per-leg parameters for each side...

Writing leg sweep code...

Checking the claw spike direction stays within floor bounds, the drop is small enough to stay valid, then moving to add tibia spikes at two points along the chain.

Confirming the spike helper's signature takes base, direction, length, and radius through an options object, then finalizing the leg geometry and exporting the root mesh with metadata.
